title: How do you design pagination in a REST API: query-parameter-based (`?page=2&size=20` or `?offset=40&limit=20`), returning metadata (`totalElements`, `totalPages`, `hasNext`), and why does offset pagination break at deep pages (use cursor/keyset instead: `?after=lastSeenId&limit=20`)?
shortTitle: How do you design pagination in a REST API and why does offset pagination break at deep pages

s1_definition.oneliner: Offset pagination is simple but slows down at deep pages because the database skips all preceding rows; cursor or keyset pagination stays fast by jumping to the slice after the last seen key.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Offset pagination** – uses query parameters like `?page=2&size=20` or `?offset=40&limit=20`; the database uses `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` in SQL.
- **Metadata** – the response includes `totalElements`, `totalPages`, `hasNext`, `hasPrevious` so the client can build navigation.
- **Deep-page problem** – `OFFSET 49980` forces the database to scan and discard 49,980 rows before returning 20, so cost grows linearly with depth.
- **Cursor (keyset) pagination** – remembers the last seen key and queries `WHERE id > :lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`, using an index seek that is fast at any depth.
- **Trade-off** – cursor pagination cannot jump to an arbitrary page number; offset pagination can but degrades at depth.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh asks National Bank of India for his transaction history, and he has fifty thousand transactions. The bank cannot hand him all fifty thousand on one screen, so it gives him twenty at a time, like pages in a passbook. That is pagination. But if he jumps to page two thousand, the clerk has to count past the first thirty-nine thousand entries just to find where to start, which is painfully slow. The smarter way is to remember the last transaction he saw and say "give me the twenty after TXN-39980," so the clerk jumps straight there. That is cursor pagination.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Pagination returns a large result set in smaller navigable chunks. The common form is offset-based, where the client sends page and size, and the server uses `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` in SQL. The response includes metadata like total elements, total pages, and hasNext. In Spring Data, a repository method taking a `Pageable` returns a `Page` that carries both content and metadata.

Offset pagination breaks at deep pages for three reasons. Performance: `OFFSET 49980` forces the database to scan and discard 49,980 rows. Cost: the total count requires a separate full-table scan. Correctness: inserts and deletes shift offsets, causing duplicates or gaps. Cursor pagination fixes all three by querying `WHERE id > :lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`, which uses an index seek that is constant-time at any depth and stable under concurrent writes.

At National Bank of India, offset pagination was instant on page one but crawled when power users scrolled to page two thousand, and incoming transactions caused duplicate entries across pages. The team switched transaction history and audit logs to cursor pagination, fetching one extra row to detect hasNext without a count, and kept offset pagination only on the admin screen where users need jump-to-page.

The judgement is that cursor pagination trades the ability to jump to an arbitrary page for constant-time deep access and stability under concurrent writes. Use offset where jump-to-page matters and the data is small, and cursor where the data is large and append-heavy. In both cases, cap the maximum page size so a client can never request unbounded results.

Remember one sentence: offset pagination degrades linearly at depth because the database skips rows, while cursor pagination uses an index seek to stay fast at any depth.

---

keyPoints: Offset pagination uses LIMIT and OFFSET in SQL and includes metadata like totalElements, totalPages, and hasNext.
Offset pagination degrades at deep pages because the database must scan and discard all preceding rows.
Cursor (keyset) pagination queries forward from the last seen key, using an index seek that is fast at any depth.
Cursor pagination is stable under concurrent inserts because it anchors on a value, not a position.
Use offset for small tables where jump-to-page is needed, and cursor for large, append-heavy data like transaction history.
Always cap the maximum page size to prevent clients from requesting unbounded results.
